items.heading: At the Start
items.text: At the start of a career, most decisions are cheap to reverse. A wrong first job costs a year, not a decade.

items.heading: Use the 5 Mid
items.text: Use The 5 Mid-Career Levers as a checklist, not a sequence you must complete in order. Most professionals only need to actively work one or two of these at a time, the framework is here so you diagnose the right one instead of guessing.

items.heading: This Is the Debate That
items.text: This is the debate that most mid-career professionals circle without resolving: keep narrowing into one specialty, or widen out and become someone who connects several areas. The honest answer is that pure specialists and pure generalists both carry real risk at this stage, a narrow specialist can be displaced if that one specialty flattens or automates, and a broad generalist without depth anywhere struggles to stand out for anything specific. The model that tends to hold up best in the research on this is the T-shaped professional: real depth in one area, plus a working ability to connect it to two or three adjacent areas.

items.heading: Job
items.text: Job-to-job moves inside the same field need the smallest buffer, three to six months of expenses usually covers the realistic gap, since a comparable role is typically the fastest kind of move to close.

items.heading: A Sabbatical or an Extended
items.text: A sabbatical or an extended break needs six to twelve months of expenses, plus a separate line item for individual health insurance, since employer group cover generally stops the moment you stop being an employee, a cost people forget until a medical bill arrives mid-break.

items.heading: A Field Pivot or Starting
items.text: A field pivot or starting something independent needs the widest buffer of all, closer to twelve months, because income during the ramp-up is unpredictable rather than simply delayed.
